entries.question: Ari has searched their library this turn with [Bog Glider]. During their end step, Nico casts [Mission Briefing]. Can they use it to cast [Archive Trap] from their graveyard for free?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling as the reference: Mission Briefing lets Nico cast Archive Trap from their graveyard this turn and, because Ari (an opponent) searched their library, Nico may pay the trap alternative cost of {0}.
entries.answer:
Yes. Nico may use Mission Briefing to cast Archive Trap from Nico’s graveyard and may pay {0} rather than Archive Trap’s mana cost, because Ari’s earlier search with Bog Glider counts as “an opponent searched their library this turn” for Archive Trap’s trap condition and Mission Briefing allows Nico to cast the chosen instant or sorcery from the graveyard this turn.

Reasoning and rules applied
- Define “search”: A spell or ability causes a player to search their library only if it specifically contains the word “search” in its text; Bog Glider’s ability says “Search your library…,” so Ari’s use of Bog Glider earlier this turn was a search and therefore counts as a library search this turn ([Archive Trap ruling #6]; Bog Glider). 
- Mission Briefing lets its controller cast a chosen instant or sorcery from their graveyard “this turn,” so Nico is allowed to begin to cast Archive Trap from Nico’s graveyard this turn (Mission Briefing; [Mission Briefing ruling #3]; see rule 601.3e about being allowed to cast a spell). 
- Archive Trap’s trap alternative cost reads “If an opponent searched their library this turn, you may pay {0} rather than pay this spell’s mana cost.” Archive Trap’s rules clarify that the trap condition checks only whether an opponent searched their library this turn (not whether they found anything), so Ari’s search with Bog Glider satisfies that condition for Nico if Ari is an opponent of Nico ([Archive Trap ruling #5]; [Archive Trap ruling #6]; Archive Trap). 
- Alternative costs are applied when a spell is cast; casting a spell for its alternative (trap) cost follows the normal rules for alternative costs and determining total cost (rules 118.9b and 601.2f). Therefore Nico may choose to pay {0} as Archive Trap’s cost when casting it from the graveyard this turn. 
- Note: You may instead cast Archive Trap for its normal mana cost if you prefer ([Archive Trap ruling #4]).

Multiplayer note: This answer assumes Ari is an opponent of Nico. In a multiplayer game, Archive Trap’s trap condition is satisfied only if any opponent of Nico searched their library this turn; if Ari is not an opponent of Nico, Ari’s search would not meet Archive Trap’s condition for Nico ([Archive Trap ruling #5]).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Mission Briefing allows Nico to cast Archive Trap from their graveyard, without any other restrictions on how it's cast. Nico can choose to pay the alternative cost of {0}.

entries.question: Avalyn has no cards in their library and controls a [Keranos, God of Storms]. What happens at the beginning of their draw step?

entries.answer:
Avalyn attempts to draw for their draw step, can’t because their library is empty, and will lose the game the next time a player would receive priority; Keranos, God of Storms’s reveal-and-trigger ability does not do anything because there was no card drawn to reveal. 

Reasoning and definitions: A “state-based action” is a game action that happens automatically whenever certain conditions are met and doesn’t use the stack [704.1]. The draw step’s first turn-based action is that the active player draws a card [504.1]; turn-based actions are performed when a step begins before state-based actions are checked [703.3]. If a player attempts to draw a card from a library with no cards in it, that player will lose the game the next time a player would receive priority (this is handled as a state-based action) [121.4, 704.5b]. After the turn-based draw action is performed and the game would next give out priority, state-based actions are checked and performed, causing Avalyn to lose at that time [704.3, 117.5]. 

Keranos, God of Storms’s text instructs you to reveal the first card you draw on each of your turns and creates effects based on what is revealed; because no card was drawn there is nothing to reveal and none of those reveal-triggered effects occur (see Keranos, God of Storms) [Keranos, God of Storms]. For reference, if a card were revealed and it were a land, Keranos, God of Storms’s ruling notes that would cause you to draw another card, but that is irrelevant here because no draw occurred [Keranos, God of Storms ruling #9].
entries.answer_gold: Avalyn can't draw a card, so no card is revealed and neither trigger triggers. Avalyn loses the game before they would next get priority.

entries.question: Amina attacks with [Retaliation]. Nico declares no blocks and then casts [Curtain of Light] targeting Retaliation. Does Retaliation trigger?

No — Retaliation’s granted ability does not trigger. Curtain of Light makes the attacking creature become blocked without causing any creature to become a blocking creature, and Retaliation’s ability requires the creature to “become blocked by a creature.”

Reasoning and definitions (short):
- “Becomes blocked” / “blocked creature”: An attacking creature becomes a blocked creature when one or more creatures are declared as blockers for it, and it remains blocked unless removed from combat or an effect changes that (rule 509.1h).
- “Becomes blocked by a creature”: An ability that triggers when a creature becomes blocked by a creature requires a creature to become a blocking creature for that attacker at the moment the blocker is declared (rule 509.3f).
- Curtain of Light’s text and rulings: Curtain of Light’s effect is “Target unblocked attacking creature becomes blocked,” and it can be cast after blockers are declared; Curtain of Light does cause “becomes blocked” events that trigger abilities that care only about “becomes blocked” (for example, it does trigger bushido abilities) ([Curtain of Light ruling #1], [Curtain of Light ruling #2]).
- Trigger condition check: A triggered ability only triggers if its trigger event actually occurs (rule 603.2g). Because no creature actually became a blocking creature when Curtain of Light resolved, the specific event “this creature becomes blocked by a creature” did not occur, so the ability granted by Retaliation (“Whenever this creature becomes blocked by a creature, this creature gets +1/+1 until end of turn.”) does not trigger (Retaliation; 509.3f; 509.1h; 603.2g).

Assumption and alternative timing: This answer assumes the sequence you described (Nico declares no blockers, then casts and resolves Curtain of Light during combat after blockers are declared). If instead some actual creature later becomes a blocking creature for the attacking creature (i.e., a creature is declared or otherwise caused to block), then the Retaliation-granted ability would trigger at the moment that creature becomes a blocking creature for the attacker (rule 509.3f).
entries.answer_gold: No. Retaliation became blocked, but not by any creatures.

entries.question: Alivia has [Road // Ruin] in their graveyard. Alivia casts [Torrential Gearhulk]. Which side of Road // Ruin can Alivia cast with its trigger?

Why: While Road // Ruin is in the graveyard it has the combined characteristics of both halves, so it can be targeted as an instant card (Road // Ruin ruling #3). Also, if you cast the card with Torrential Gearhulk’s ability, you cast it as part of that ability’s resolution (Torrential Gearhulk ruling #0).

entries.question: Alfred casts [Stream of Thought], replicating it twice. Nico controls [Chalice of the Void] with 1 charge counter. What happens?

Alfred’s two replicate copies of Stream of Thought are created and resolve first; after those copies resolve, Chalice of the Void’s triggered ability will counter the original Stream of Thought (the original spell itself does not resolve).

Why: Replicate means “When you cast this spell, if a replicate cost was paid for it, copy it for each time its replicate cost was paid” and Alfred paid Stream of Thought’s replicate cost twice, so two copies are created when Stream of Thought was cast [702.56a]. The copy effect created by replicate puts copies of Stream of Thought onto the stack; a copy of a spell is not cast (it’s put onto the stack by the copy effect) [707.10]. Chalice of the Void’s ability triggers only when a player casts a spell with mana value equal to its charge counters, so it triggered when Alfred cast Stream of Thought (Stream of Thought’s mana value is 1), and that triggered ability can counter the original Stream of Thought when that trigger resolves (Chalice of the Void’s text).

Stream of Thought’s replicate-related rulings make the interaction clear: you get a copy for each time you paid the replicate cost even if the original spell is later countered [Stream of Thought ruling #3], and if you replicate Stream of Thought the copies resolve before the original spell, so those copies can’t shuffle the original Stream of Thought into your library while the original is still on the stack [Stream of Thought ruling #1]. Practically, the two copies each resolve (each copy mills the chosen target player for four and then allows Alfred to shuffle up to four cards from Alfred’s graveyard into Alfred’s library, though not the original Stream of Thought because it’s still on the stack), and later the Chalice of the Void triggered ability resolves and counters the original Stream of Thought, so the original does nothing further.

Assumption about timing: this answer assumes the normal ordering where triggered abilities created by casting Stream of Thought (the replicate copy-creating trigger) and Chalet of the Void’s triggered ability are placed on the stack and then resolve; the rulings cited determine that the replicate copies resolve before the original regardless of the original being countered [Stream of Thought ruling #1, Stream of Thought ruling #3]. If an alternative trigger-ordering detail were specified, the end result (copies still resolve; the original is countered) is unchanged because of those rulings.
entries.answer_gold: The original Stream of Thought is countered, the two copies resolve as normal. Replicate and Chalice of the Void both trigger when the spell is cast. Since the Chalice of the Void trigger is controlled by the player last in turn order, it will resolve first, countering Stream of Thought. Then Stream of Thought's trigger resolves and creates two copies of Stream of Thought. The copies are not cast, so they don't trigger Chalice of the Void.

entries.question: Autumn controls [Captain Mar-Vell, Space-Born] and casts [Tempted by the Oriq] targeting Breanna's and Case's Soldier tokens. Before it resolves, Autumn casts [Insurrection]. What happens?

Direct answer: Insurrection resolves first (it was cast in response), so Autumn gains control of all creatures until end of turn (that includes Breanna’s Soldier token and Case’s Soldier token). After Insurrection resolves, Tempted by the Oriq checks its targets and finds that the chosen creatures are no longer creatures “that [Breanna/Case] control,” so Tempted by the Oriq has no legal targets for those instances and therefore doesn’t resolve; put Tempted by the Oriq into Autumn’s graveyard and no control-change from that spell happens.

Why: “In response to” means a spell cast while another is on the stack goes on top and will resolve first (117.7, 405.2). When the players let the stack resolve, the topmost object resolves first (608.1, 405.5). Insurrection’s text is “Untap all creatures and gain control of them until end of turn. They gain haste until end of turn,” so when Insurrection resolves Autumn gains control of all creatures, including the two Soldier tokens (Insurrection card data). When Tempted by the Oriq tries to resolve, the game checks whether its targets are still legal. A target that is no longer controlled by the player referenced by the spell is an illegal target; if all targets for every instance of the word “target” are illegal, the spell doesn’t resolve and, if it’s a spell, it’s put into its owner’s graveyard (608.2b). Because Autumn now controls those tokens, they are no longer legal targets for the parts of Tempted by the Oriq that say “target creature or planeswalker that player controls with mana value 3 or less,” so Tempted by the Oriq doesn’t resolve (Tempted by the Oriq card data, 608.2b).

Assumption/Timing note: This assumes the sequence you described (Autumn casts Tempted by the Oriq, then while it’s on the stack Autumn casts Insurrection “in response” to it). If instead Insurrection had resolved earlier (before Tempted by the Oriq was cast), the same end result applies at resolution time because target legality is always checked when Tempted by the Oriq resolves (608.2b).
entries.answer_gold: Insurrection resolves and Autumn gains control of all the Soldier tokens. Then Tempted by the Oriq begins to resolve, but its targets are now illegal, so it does not resolve and is removed from the stack.

entries.question: Amelia casts [Aminatou's Augury] exiling an artifact and an instant. Afterwards Amelia casts another Aminatou's Augury, which exiles an instant. Can they cast both instants?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude each Aminatou's Augury creates its own permission tied to the cards it exiled, so casting the instant from one doesn't prevent casting the instant exiled by the other.
entries.answer:
Yes. Amelia may cast both instants: the instant exiled by the first Aminatou's Augury and the instant exiled by the second Aminatou's Augury, each under the permission created by the Aminatou's Augury that exiled it. 

Definition (linked abilities): A “linked” pair of abilities is when an object’s printed ability exiles one or more cards and another printed ability on the same object refers to the exiled cards; the second ability refers only to the cards exiled by that object [607.2a].

Why: Each resolution of Aminatou's Augury exiles its own set of cards and creates the permission that lets you cast spells of those nonland types from among the cards it exiled until end of turn. Because those abilities are linked to the specific Aminatou's Augury that exiled those cards, the first Aminatou's Augury’s permission applies to the instant it exiled and the second Aminatou's Augury’s permission applies to the instant it exiled [607.2a]. Casting one of those exiled instants causes that card to leave exile when you cast it, and you can’t cast that same exiled card multiple times [Aminatou's Augury ruling #6]; that doesn’t stop you from also casting the other instant that was exiled by the other Aminatou's Augury. To actually cast those instants you must have priority and follow the normal casting process (moving the card from exile to the stack and paying any costs — here the Augury permissions waive the mana cost) [117.1a; 601.2a; 601.3f].

Timing note: This assumes you cast both instants before the “until end of turn” window from the relevant Aminatou's Augury effects expires. You need priority to cast each instant when you attempt to do so [117.1a].
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Each Aminatou's Augury creates a separate effect that applies to cards it exiled. Casting an instant off the first Aminatou's Augury doesn't preclude Amelia from casting an instant off the second one.

entries.question: Aranza controls a [Welding Jar] enchanted by Nico's [Curse Artifact]. In response to the trigger during Aranza's upkeep, Nico casts [Word of Seizing] to take control of the Welding Jar. What happens as the trigger resolves?

If, instead, Word of Seizing had not resolved before the triggered ability resolved (for example, if Nico hadn’t cast it in response), Aranza would still control Welding Jar and could choose to sacrifice Welding Jar to avoid the 2 damage when the triggered ability resolved.
entries.answer_gold: Aranza is dealt 2 damage. Sacrificing the Welding Jar is a cost. If the cost isn't paid, the default action of dealing 2 damage to Aranza happens. Aranza cannot sacrifice a permanent that they don't control.

entries.question: Amos controls [March of the Machines] and [Mycosynth Lattice] and casts [Lust for War] targeting their [Gilded Sentinel]. What will happen when Lust for War resolves?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly says Lust for War enters attached and only becomes unattached at the next SBA check before going to the graveyard, while the correct ruling is it can't legally enchant on resolution and is put directly into its owner's graveyard.
entries.answer:
When Lust for War resolves, Lust for War will enter the battlefield attached to Gilded Sentinel, but because Mycosynth Lattice makes Lust for War an artifact and March of the Machines makes noncreature artifacts into artifact creatures, Lust for War becomes an Aura that is also a creature, so Lust for War can’t enchant anything; it becomes unattached at the next state-based actions check and is then put into its owner’s graveyard. 

Reasoning and definitions
- Lust for War is an Aura that enters the battlefield attached to the targeted creature when its spell resolves (Lust for War). 
- Mycosynth Lattice makes all permanents artifacts in addition to their other types (Mycosynth Lattice). That causes Lust for War to be an artifact as soon as it’s a permanent. 
- March of the Machines makes each noncreature artifact an artifact creature with power and toughness equal to its mana value (March of the Machines). Once Lust for War is an artifact permanent and is not a creature by its text, it is a noncreature artifact and becomes an artifact creature under March of the Machines. 
- An Aura that’s also a creature can’t enchant anything; such an Aura is unattached the next time state-based actions are checked and is then put into its owner’s graveyard as a second state-based action (Mycosynth Lattice ruling #0). 

So the timeline is: Lust for War resolves and enters attached to Gilded Sentinel; continuous effects from Mycosynth Lattice and March of the Machines immediately make Lust for War an artifact creature Aura; because an Aura that’s a creature can’t be attached as an Aura, Lust for War becomes unattached at the next state-based actions check and is then put into its owner’s graveyard.

If anything else changes the object’s characteristics or attachments between resolution and the state-based actions check, those changes would be applied before the unattaching and putting into the graveyard, but the ruling above governs the normal outcome.
entries.answer_gold: Lust for War cannot legally enchant anything, so it will be put directly into its owners graveyard.

entries.question: Avery controls [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathan casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics after Turn to Frog resolves?

Direct answer: After Turn to Frog resolves, Wayward Angel is a blue Frog creature with no abilities and has base power and toughness 1/1, and it then gets +3/+3 from its threshold, so its final power/toughness is 4/4. It is not white (it’s blue), and it has no flying, vigilance, trample, or the “At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature” triggered ability.

Reasoning and steps (rules used):
- “Characteristics” are determined by starting with the actual object (the printed Wayward Angel card) and then applying all applicable continuous effects in layers (see 613.1g).  
- Turn to Frog’s effect makes the targeted permanent “lose all abilities and becomes a blue Frog with base power and toughness 1/1.” That effect sets the creature’s base power and toughness to 1/1 and makes it blue Frog when it resolves (see Turn to Frog ruling #1 and Turn to Frog ruling #5).  
- Effects that set a creature’s base power and toughness are applied in layer 7b; other power/toughness modifications (such as “gets +3/+3”) are applied later in the layer series (see 613.4b and 613.1g). Turn to Frog therefore sets Wayward Angel’s base P/T to 1/1, and Wayward Angel’s threshold “gets +3/+3” then modifies that, producing a final P/T of 4/4 (Turn to Frog overwrote any earlier base-setting effects, per Turn to Frog ruling #1).  
- Wayward Angel’s threshold text makes Wayward Angel black while the threshold condition is met (Wayward Angel ruling #0). Turn to Frog makes the creature blue; continuous effects that change the same characteristic are applied in layers/timestamp order, so the later (Turn to Frog) color-setting effect results in Wayward Angel being blue after Turn to Frog resolves (613.1g; see also the Turn to Frog ruling #5 example showing Turn to Frog producing a blue creature).  
- Turn to Frog causes the creature to “lose all abilities,” so Wayward Angel loses its abilities (flying, vigilance), loses trample granted by threshold, and loses the triggered upkeep ability granted by threshold. (See Turn to Frog ruling #5 that the affected permanent will have no abilities; Turn to Frog ruling #3 notes that abilities gained after Turn to Frog resolves are kept, which is why the removal is tied to the moment Turn to Frog’s effect is applied.)

Timing note/assumption: This answer assumes Turn to Frog resolves while Wayward Angel’s controller still has seven or more cards in their graveyard (so the threshold condition is satisfied both before and after Turn to Frog resolves). If the graveyard count changes so the threshold condition no longer holds at the moment effects are applied, the +3/+3 and the threshold-granted pieces would not be present.
entries.answer_gold: It's a 4/4 blue Frog with no abilities. Wayward Angel's last ability begins to apply in layer 5. It's removed by Turn to Frog in layer 6, but since it's already started to apply, it will continue doing so in later layers. Wayward Angel has the earlier timestamp, so it gives itself trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature" before Turn to Frog removes its abilities in layer 6.

entries.question: Autumn, Bethany, and Chaim started playing a multiplayer game. Chaim lost the game, and then Autumn restarted the game with [Karn Liberated]. Will Autumn draw a card on the first turn of the restarted game?

Definitions and reasoning
- “Restarting the game” means the current game immediately ends and all players who were in that game when it ended begin a new game following the normal game-start procedures, except that the starting player in the new game is the player who controlled the spell or ability that restarted the game (Karn Liberated). See [727.1a] and [Karn Liberated ruling #2].
- The draw step’s turn-based action is that the active player draws a card immediately after the draw step begins (this action doesn’t use the stack). See [504.1] and [703.4d].
- Because any player who left the game before Karn Liberated’s ability restarted it isn’t involved in the new game, Chaim (who lost and left before the restart) won’t be in the new game. See [Karn Liberated ruling #9].
- Therefore Autumn is the starting player of the new multiplayer game (controller of Karn Liberated’s restart ability) and, under multiplayer rules, the starting player does not skip the draw step of their first turn. See [727.1a], [Karn Liberated ruling #2], and [800.7].

Assumption: I’m assuming the question means the first turn of the new game that began when Autumn used Karn Liberated’s −14 ability; if the timing were meant differently, say a separate extra turn effect after the restart, the same draw-step rules above would be applied to that turn’s draw step instead.
entries.answer_gold: No. The game began with 2 players, so it is a two-player game.. Autumn will skip their draw step.

entries.question: Addison casts [Virulent Wound], targeting Natalee's [Memnite]. In response, Natalee casts [Resounding Roar] on the Memnite. What happens at the end of the turn?

entries.answer:
Answer: Natalee’s Memnite ends up in Natalee’s graveyard during the cleanup step, and Natalee gets a poison counter from Virulent Wound.

Reasoning and definitions:
- Resounding Roar gives the targeted creature +3/+3 until end of turn (Resounding Roar).  That makes Natalee’s Memnite a 4/4 (base 1/1 +3/+3). (I assume Resounding Roar resolves before Virulent Wound because Natalee cast Resounding Roar in response to Addison casting Virulent Wound.)
- When Virulent Wound resolves, it puts a -1/-1 counter on the targeted creature and creates the ability “When that creature dies this turn, its controller gets a poison counter” (Virulent Wound).
- After Virulent Wound resolves, Natalee’s Memnite is 3/3 (1/1 +3/+3 then one -1/-1 counter). It is not put into a graveyard at that moment.
- At cleanup, all “until end of turn” and “this turn” effects end simultaneously (703.4p, 514.2). Resounding Roar’s +3/+3 ends, so Natalee’s Memnite becomes a 0/0 (1/1 minus the one -1/-1 counter).
- A creature with toughness 0 or less is put into its owner’s graveyard by state-based actions (704.5f). That is when Natalee’s Memnite is put into Natalee’s graveyard (it “dies” that turn).
- Because Virulent Wound specified “When that creature dies this turn, its controller gets a poison counter,” and the creature is put into a graveyard on the same turn Virulent Wound resolved, Natalee gets a poison counter (Virulent Wound ruling #0).

Key term definitions:
- “Until end of turn” effect: an effect that lasts until the cleanup step of the current turn and ends during that cleanup step (703.4p, 514.2).
- “Dies” / “is put into a graveyard”: for this interaction, “dies this turn” means the creature is put into a graveyard from the battlefield during the same turn Virulent Wound resolved (Virulent Wound; 704.5f).

Timing note: I assumed the spells resolved in the order implied (Resounding Roar resolves before Virulent Wound because it was cast in response). If instead Resounding Roar somehow failed to resolve before Virulent Wound, the outcomes could differ (for example, the -1/-1 counter might immediately make Natalee’s Memnite die before any +3/+3 is applied).
entries.answer_gold: The effect from Resounding Roar wears off, but the -1/-1 counter remains. Memnite dies. The delayed triggered ability created by Virulent Wound is not a continuous effect, so it still exists during the cleanup step, and will trigger due to Memnite dying. Natalee gets a poison counter.

entries.question: Amaris, Blaine, and Clyde begin a multiplayer game. In Amaris's upkeep, they use [Leyline of Anticipation], several [Simian Spirit Guide]s and [Desperate Ritual]s, and [Goblin Charbelcher] to kill Blaine. Does Amaris draw a card for the turn?

entries.question: Allyson controls [Ice Cauldron]. Nico controls [Suppression Field]. Allyson activates Ice Cauldron's first ability with X=1, paying {C}{C}{C}. On Allyson's next turn, they activate Ice Cauldron's second ability. How much mana do they add?

Why: Suppression Field’s static ability makes activated abilities cost {2} more to activate unless they’re mana abilities, so when Allyson activated Ice Cauldron’s first ability with X = 1 she paid {1} for X plus the extra {2} from Suppression Field, for a total of {C}{C}{C} spent to activate that ability. entries.question: Aimee controls a manifested [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Noah casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. After that resolves, Aimee turns Wayward Angel face up. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics afterwards?

After Wayward Angel is turned face up, Wayward Angel is a black Frog creature with power/toughness 4/4 and it has trample and “At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature.” Wayward Angel does not have flying or vigilance and is not white.

Wayward Angel receives a new timestamp when it turns face up, so its ability is applied before Turn to Frog in each layer. Wayward Angel's last ability is removed by Turn to Frog in layer 6, but since it's already started to apply in layer 5 to change its color to black, it will continue doing so in later layers. Turn to Frog has the earlier timestamp, so it makes Wayward Angel blue before it becomes black in layer 5 and removes Wayward Angel's abilities in layer 6 before it gains trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature".

entries.question: Bobbie has 1 life and controls a phased-out [Angel of Sanctions] that exiled Conrad's [Rotted Hystrix]. Alana casts [Lava Axe], targeting Bobbie. What happens as Bobbie loses the game?

When Bobbie loses the game, Bobbie’s phased-out Angel of Sanctions leaves the game and Conrad’s Rotted Hystrix returns to the battlefield immediately under Conrad’s control. The return is the one-shot effect tied to Angel of Sanctions leaving and does not go on the stack.

- “Leaves the game”: When a player leaves the game, all objects owned by that player leave the game and effects giving that player control of objects end; these things happen immediately (rule 800.4a; see also rule 405.6h about such actions not using the stack). 
- “Phased-out permanent”: A permanent that is phased out. Phased-out permanents owned by a player who leaves the game also leave the game (rule 702.26k).

- I assume Lava Axe resolves and the resulting state causes Bobbie to lose and leave the game; the rest follows as described. If the loss happened for another simultaneous reason, the same “player leaves the game → owned objects leave the game → exiled card returns” sequence applies per the cited rules.

entries.question: Aubrey controls [Mycosynth Lattice]. Natalia controls [Watchwolf] enchanted with [Favorable Destiny]. Aubrey casts [Opportunistic Dragon] and takes control of Favorable Destiny. What will happen after Opportunistic Dragon's ability resolves?

Why: Mycosynth Lattice makes permanents into artifacts, so Favorable Destiny is a legal target for Opportunistic Dragon's triggered ability (see Mycosynth Lattice and Opportunistic Dragon). Because Favorable Destiny has been made to “lose all abilities” by Opportunistic Dragon's continuous effect, Favorable Destiny's text (“Enchanted creature gets +1/+2 as long as it's white” and “Enchanted creature has shroud as long as its controller controls another creature”) no longer functions while Opportunistic Dragon remains on the battlefield, so those bonuses and shroud do not apply to Natalia's Watchwolf. (Separately, Mycosynth Lattice makes permanents colorless, so Watchwolf is not white under Mycosynth Lattice; even if Favorable Destiny still had abilities, the +1/+2 condition would not be met.)
entries.answer_gold: Favorable Destiny will continue to be attached to Watchwolf indefinitely. The "enchant" keyword is a restriction on what an Aura can enchant- without it Favorable Destiny is legally able to enchant anything.

entries.question: Alaia controls [Panharmonicon] and [Mycosynth Lattice] and has [Minotaur Warrior] and [Ogre Resister] in their graveyard. They cast [Dance of the Dead] targeting Minotaur Warrior. What happens as it enters the battlefield?

entries.question: Adelaide casts a [Keldon Champion]. In response, Nico casts [Hallow], targeting the Keldon Champion. When Adelaide attacks with the Keldon Champion that turn, will the damage be prevented?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Hallow won't prevent the Keldon Champion's later damage, which directly contradicts the reference's ruling that the prevention effect carries over to the permanent.
entries.answer: No. Hallow’s prevention will not stop damage dealt later by Keldon Champion when it attacks that turn. Hallow (“Prevent all damage target spell would deal this turn. entries.question: Autumn casts [Time Stretch]. Can they choose to skip both extra turns with [Time Vault]?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the opposite conclusion—saying you can skip at most one extra turn—while the reference says you can skip both extra turns.
entries.answer:
No. Autumn can’t use Time Vault to skip both extra turns granted by Time Stretch; at most one of those extra turns can be skipped with Time Vault.

Reasoning: Time Stretch gives the targeted player two extra turns after this one (see Time Stretch). Extra turns are added one at a time (rule 500.7). A “skip [turn]” effect is a replacement effect that is applied as a turn would begin (rules 614.10 and 614.1); Time Vault’s text and ruling say that the choice to skip is made as that turn would begin and only if Time Vault is tapped at that time, and if you choose to skip that turn Time Vault untaps before anything else happens in the next turn (Time Vault ruling #1). Therefore, if Autumn uses Time Vault’s “If you would begin your turn while this artifact is tapped, you may skip that turn instead. If you do, untap this artifact.” choice to skip the first extra turn, Time Vault will untap before the following extra turn begins, so it won’t be tapped at the beginning of the second extra turn and its skip option can’t apply to that second extra turn. (If Autumn instead declines to skip the first extra turn and Time Vault is still tapped at the beginning of the second extra turn, Autumn could then choose to skip that second extra turn.)

Assumption: I assume the normal timing where the two extra turns from Time Stretch are the next two turns to be taken by Autumn after the current turn; the same conclusion holds because extra turns are added one at a time (rule 500.7). If the timing of when the extra turns occur were different, the ruling about when the skip choice is made (Time Vault ruling #1) still governs each turn’s beginning.
entries.answer_gold: Yes. As their turn ends, they can apply Time Vault's replacement effect, which means the next turn gets skipped and Time Vault gets untapped as part of the next turn that actually happens. Then, since it's still tapped as Autumn's turn is ending, they can choose to skip the next turn again.
